questions.s: Concerning the general topography of the neck (Last's):
o: The hard palate lies level with the anterior arch of the atlas
The lower border of the mandible lies between C2 and C3. (Last's p. 421)
Levator scapulae is supplied by posterior rami as part of the extensor mass
It belongs to the prevertebral flexor group supplied by anterior rami. (Last's p. 421)
The anterior part of the neck extends no higher than mylohyoid
Further back the neck reaches the skull base. (Last's p. 421)
Last's describes three parts to the deep cervical fascia
Four: investing, pretracheal, prevertebral and the carotid sheath. (Last's p. 421)
The deep part of the parotid capsule is thickened as the stylomandibular ligament
It runs from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible. (Last's p. 422)
The suprasternal space lies between the investing and pretracheal layers
It lies between two layers of the split investing layer attached to the front and back of the jugular notch. (Last's p. 422)
The deeper investing layer above the middle clavicle forms a sling for the inferior belly of omohyoid
The two layers correspond to the clavipectoral fascia layers around subclavius. (Last's p. 422-3)
The superficial part of the parotid capsule is thin
It is thick and forms the parotid fascia, attached to the zygomatic arch. (Last's p. 422)
The prevertebral fascia extends down to the body of T3
The lower limit of longus colli. (Last's p. 423)
The prevertebral fascia invests the subclavian vein
It covers the third part of the subclavian artery but not the vein, which lies free to dilate. (Last's p. 423)
The accessory nerve in the posterior triangle lies superficial to the prevertebral fascia
So do the posterior triangle lymph nodes. (Last's p. 423)
The prevertebral fascia extends laterally to the posterior border of trapezius
It fades out well under cover of the anterior border of trapezius. (Last's p. 423)

questions.s: Concerning the pretracheal fascia and carotid sheath (Last's):
o: The pretracheal fascia adheres to the thyroid only between the isthmus and tracheal rings 2–4
Elsewhere it is not adherent. (Last's p. 423)
The pretracheal fascia is attached above to the hyoid along its whole width
Laterally it reaches only the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, limited by the strap muscles. (Last's p. 423)
Last's says the carotid sheath is not a demonstrable membranous layer
It is a feltwork of areolar tissue, thin over the internal jugular vein. (Last's p. 423)
The cervical sympathetic trunk lies within the carotid sheath
It lies behind it, attached to the front of the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 423)

questions.s: Concerning the tissue spaces of the neck (Last's):
o: A cervical vertebral abscess behind the prevertebral fascia can track to T3
No lower unless the fascia gives way. (Last's p. 423)
The retropharyngeal space ends at the root of the neck
The space in front of the prevertebral fascia extends from the skull base to the diaphragm. (Last's p. 423)
Last's says there is no anatomical barrier to retropharyngeal spread into the mediastinum
Pathological walling off usually prevents it. (Last's p. 424)
The parapharyngeal space is bounded laterally by the buccopharyngeal fascia
It is bounded laterally by the pterygoid muscles and parotid sheath. (Last's p. 424)
The clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid is a thick fleshy mass
The manubrial head is a rounded tendon. (Last's p. 424)
The accessory nerve emerges from sternocleidomastoid about a third of the way down its posterior border
It emerges about halfway down. (Last's p. 424)
The anterior horn cells for sternocleidomastoid are controlled by the ipsilateral cortex
Trapezius has the usual contralateral innervation. (Last's p. 424)
The cervical plexus branches to sternocleidomastoid are motor
They are proprioceptive only; motor is the accessory, mostly C2 and 3. (Last's p. 424)
Sternocleidomastoid is the principal rotator at the lateral atlantoaxial joint
The face turns to the opposite side. (Last's p. 425)
Contraction of one sternocleidomastoid turns the chin to the same side
The ear approaches the shoulder and the chin rotates to the opposite side. (Last's p. 424)
Opposite splenius capitis produces the same wry neck position as one sternocleidomastoid
(Last's p. 424)
The chief action of both muscles is pure flexion of the head on the atlas
Last's: the chief purpose is protraction — neck flexion with atlanto-occipital extension. (Last's p. 425)
The accessory nerve disappears beneath trapezius about 5 cm above the clavicle
Its line runs from the atlas transverse process. (Last's p. 426)
The accessory nerve lies deep to the prevertebral fascia
It is embedded in the fascia of the roof, separated from levator scapulae by the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 426)
The supraclavicular nodes are outlying members of the lower deep cervical group
(Last's p. 426)
The subclavian vein is a content of the posterior triangle
It is lower still; the external jugular slips into the anterior corner. (Last's p. 426)
The cervical plexus does not actually lie in the posterior triangle
It lies on scalenus medius under the upper sternocleidomastoid. (Last's p. 426)
The inferior root of the ansa cervicalis spirals around the medial side of the internal jugular vein
It spirals around the lateral side. (Last's p. 427)
The phrenic nerve passes lateral to the ascending cervical artery
It runs lateral to medial over scalenus anterior. (Last's p. 427)
Last's says the phrenic nerve never passes in front of the subclavian vein
It is not uncommon; rarely it pierces the vein. (Last's p. 427)

questions.s: Concerning cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (Last's):
o: The lesser occipital nerve hooks around the accessory nerve
It is C2. (Last's p. 427)
The great auricular nerve supplies the whole lateral surface of the auricle
It supplies the whole cranial surface and the lateral surface below the meatus. (Last's p. 427)
The great auricular nerve supplies the deep layer of the parotid fascia
Via branches deep to the gland. (Last's p. 427)
The supraclavicular nerves are mostly C3
They are C3, 4, mostly C4. (Last's p. 427)
The lateral supraclavicular nerves reach down to the spine of the scapula
The medial group reaches the sternal angle. (Last's p. 427)
The transverse cervical nerve lies close to the transverse cervical artery
It is some distance from it; the artery is just above the clavicle. (Last's p. 427)
C3 supplies the cylindrical part of the neck
C2 the back of the neck and angle of mandible; C4 the "cape" area. (Last's p. 428)
The third occipital nerve is from the posterior ramus of C2
It is C3; the greater occipital is C2. (Last's p. 427)
The digastric tendon is held by a sling to the lesser horn of the hyoid
The stylohyoid slips play no part in holding it. (Last's p. 428)
Stylohyoid inserts into the lesser horn of the hyoid
It inserts by two slips into the base of the greater horn. (Last's p. 428)
The posterior quarter of each mylohyoid inserts into the hyoid body
The anterior three-quarters meet in a raphe. (Last's p. 428)
The nerve to mylohyoid arises after the inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen
It arises just before. (Last's p. 428)
The nerve to sternohyoid enters its lower end and supplies it C1, 2, 3 from above down
Tendinous intersections may occur. (Last's p. 429)
Sternothyroid attaches to the clavicle
It attaches below the sternoclavicular joint and has no clavicular attachment. (Last's p. 429)
Omohyoid becomes tendinous where it overlies the internal jugular vein
A useful guide at operation. (Last's p. 429)
Thyrohyoid is supplied by fibres from the hypoglossal nucleus
Its fibres hitch-hike from C1. (Last's p. 429)
Sternothyroid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis C2, 3
Sternohyoid and omohyoid are C1–3. (Last's p. 429)
Sternothyroid acts on the larynx through the hyoid
It acts directly on the thyroid cartilage; the others act via the hyoid. (Last's p. 429)
In the fetus omohyoid is attached to the medial clavicle
It migrates laterally to the scapula and may be arrested anywhere. (Last's p. 429)
The thyroid lobe extends down to the third tracheal ring
It extends as low as the sixth ring. (Last's p. 430)

questions.s: Concerning the thyroid and recurrent laryngeal nerve (Last's):
o: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is more likely to lie behind the inferior thyroid artery
On the right the chances are equal. (Last's p. 430)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve may lie in front of the pretracheal fascia
It is always behind it, including the suspensory ligament of Berry. (Last's p. 430)
If the recurrent laryngeal nerve divides, the anterior branch is motor
The posterior branch is sensory only. (Last's p. 430)
The thoracic duct arches behind the thyroid at the same level as the inferior thyroid artery
The artery arches at C6; the duct at a lower level, C7. (Last's p. 430)
The superior thyroid artery is ligated right at the upper pole
To avoid the external laryngeal nerve immediately behind it. (Last's p. 431)
The inferior thyroid artery pierces the pretracheal fascia as a single trunk
It divides outside the fascia into four or five branches; the superior artery pierces as a single vessel. (Last's p. 431)
The thyroidea ima artery occurs in about 3%
From the brachiocephalic trunk, right common carotid or arch. (Last's p. 431)
Most of the inferior thyroid venous plexus drains into the right brachiocephalic vein
Most drains into the left. (Last's p. 432)
The superior thyroid vein enters the internal jugular or facial vein in about equal proportions
The middle thyroid vein goes directly to the internal jugular. (Last's p. 431)
Most thyroid sympathetic fibres come from the superior cervical ganglion
Most come from the middle cervical ganglion with the inferior thyroid artery. (Last's p. 432)
Thyroid colloid is iodinated in the follicle, not in the cells
The thyroid is unique in storing its secretion outside the cells. (Last's p. 432)
C cells reach the follicular lumen
They lie on the outer aspects and do not reach the lumina; they are under 2% of cells. (Last's p. 432)
Levator glandulae thyroideae is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve
It lies in the pyramidal lobe. (Last's p. 431)
The pyramidal lobe usually lies to the right of the midline
Generally to the left. (Last's p. 430)
Parafollicular cells come from the ultimobranchial body
Fifth pouch; no other part of the gland comes from it. (Last's p. 432)
Thyroidectomy uses a transverse incision 2 cm below the cricoid
That is tracheostomy; thyroidectomy is 2.5 cm above the jugular notch. (Last's p. 432-3)
The superior parathyroid lies level with the first tracheal ring above the inferior thyroid artery
It is the more constant gland. (Last's p. 432)
The inferior parathyroid usually lies medial to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
It lies lateral to it, below the inferior thyroid artery. (Last's p. 432)
Both parathyroids are usually supplied by the inferior thyroid artery
(Last's p. 432)
The superior parathyroid is parathyroid III
It is IV (fourth pouch); the inferior is III. (Last's p. 433)
About 10% of inferior parathyroids lie within the thymic capsule
Because they migrate further. (Last's p. 433)
Four parathyroids are present in virtually 100% of people
In about 90%. (Last's p. 432)
After total parathyroidectomy part of a gland is implanted into brachioradialis
Easier to reach later. (Last's p. 433)
Oxyphil cells secrete PTH
Chief cells secrete PTH; oxyphil function is unknown. (Last's p. 433)
The trachea is 2 cm or more deep to the jugular notch
It passes backwards as well as downwards. (Last's p. 433)
Of the 10 cm trachea, 2 cm are in the neck
5 cm are in the neck. (Last's p. 433)
In elective tracheostomy part of the second and third rings is removed
After dividing the isthmus. (Last's p. 433)
Emergency tracheotomy is the usual emergency airway
It is usually replaced by laryngotomy through the cricothyroid ligament. (Last's p. 433)
Pus tracking laterally from the pharynx passes behind the carotid sheath
The sheath is fixed in front to sternocleidomastoid fascia. (Last's p. 434)
The carotid bifurcation is always at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage
It is frequently higher, near the greater horn of the hyoid (C3). (Last's p. 434)
The superior root of the ansa contains only C1 fibres
It leaves XII where the nerve loops below the posterior digastric. (Last's p. 434)
The common carotid gives a branch to the thyroid before bifurcating
It gives no branches proximal to its bifurcation. (Last's p. 434)
XII is found just below digastric and just above the tip of the greater horn of the hyoid
Crossing the occipital, external carotid and lingual arteries. (Last's p. 435)
The submental nodes drain only their own side
They drain across the midline, including the lower incisors and tongue tip. (Last's p. 435)
Submandibular nodes drain all teeth except the lower incisors
And all the upper lip. (Last's p. 435)
Platysma's proprioceptive fibres run with the cervical branch of VII
They run with the transverse cervical nerve. (Last's p. 434)
The nerve to mylohyoid pierces the sphenomandibular ligament
At its attachment to the lower margin of the mandibular foramen. (Last's p. 436)
The mylohyoid groove marks the lower limit of medial pterygoid
It marks the upper limit of its attachment. (Last's p. 436)
The submandibular duct is the same length as the parotid duct
Both are 5 cm. (Last's p. 436)
In the deep part of the gland the lingual nerve lies below it
The lingual nerve lies above; the duct and XII lie below. (Last's p. 436)
Lymph nodes lie within the substance of the submandibular gland
So the gland is removed in radical neck dissection. (Last's p. 436)
The submandibular skin incision is made 1 cm below the mandible
About 4 cm below, to avoid the marginal mandibular nerve. (Last's p. 437)
Some submandibular secretomotor cell bodies lie on the gland surface
Most are in the submandibular ganglion. (Last's p. 436)
The submandibular gland is purely serous in man
It is mixed mucous and serous. (Last's p. 436)
At its commencement the external carotid lies medial to the internal
It then slopes up in front of it. (Last's p. 437)
The external carotid divides behind the neck of the mandible outside the parotid
It divides within the gland. (Last's p. 437)
The external carotid gives six branches before entering the parotid
Three in front, two behind, one medial. (Last's p. 437)
The occipital artery runs along the upper border of the posterior belly of digastric
It runs along the lower border; the posterior auricular along the upper. (Last's p. 437)

questions.s: Concerning branches of the external carotid (Last's):
o: The facial artery pulse is felt 2.5 cm in front of the angle of the mandible
At the anterior border of masseter. (Last's p. 438)
The superior laryngeal artery pierces the cricothyroid membrane
It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the internal laryngeal nerve. (Last's p. 437)
XII is held down at the occipital artery by its lower sternocleidomastoid branch
The upper branch guides to XI. (Last's p. 438)
The occipital artery grooves the skull superficial to the digastric notch
It grooves the occipitomastoid suture deep to the notch. (Last's p. 438)

questions.s: Concerning branches of the external carotid (Last's):
o: The stylomastoid artery gives the stapedial artery
The remnant of the second arch artery. (Last's p. 438)
The ascending pharyngeal artery arises from the front of the external carotid
It arises from its deep aspect just above the commencement. (Last's p. 438)
The ascending pharyngeal sends meningeal branches through the hypoglossal canal
Also the foramen lacerum and jugular foramen. (Last's p. 438)
The lingual artery is crossed by XII after it passes deep to hyoglossus
XII crosses the loop superficially; hyoglossus separates them further forward. (Last's p. 437, 435)

questions.s: Concerning the carotid sinus and body (Last's):
o: The carotid body has the highest bloodflow for its size of any organ
Its glomus cells contain dopamine. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body is supplied by the vagus
Its glomus cells are innervated by IX. (Last's p. 438)
The internal carotid is lateral to the external carotid at its origin
It soon slopes posteriorly to a medial deeper level. (Last's p. 438)
The superior laryngeal nerve crosses in front of the internal carotid
It crosses obliquely behind it. (Last's p. 438)
The inferior petrosal sinus usually passes lateral to the vagus to reach the internal jugular
Sometimes medial. (Last's p. 439)
The thoracic duct crosses behind the left internal jugular at C6
At C7. (Last's p. 439)
The facial, lingual and superior thyroid veins usually join near the tip of the greater horn
(Last's p. 439)
The surface marking of the internal jugular runs from the mastoid tip to the sternal end of the clavicle
From the lobule of the ear. (Last's p. 439)
Longus capitis arises from the anterior tubercles of C3–6
In line with scalenus anterior. (Last's p. 440)
The upper fibres of longus colli run from the atlas to C5–6
Upper fibres run to C3–5; lower fibres from T1–3 to C5–6. (Last's p. 440)
The pyramidal space between longus colli and scalenus anterior has the carotid tubercle as apex
Its base is the first part of subclavian. (Last's p. 440)
Rectus capitis lateralis attaches to the front of the foramen magnum
That is rectus capitis anterior; lateralis goes to the jugular process. (Last's p. 440)
The superior cervical ganglion contains about 1 million cell bodies
It is about 3 cm long. (Last's p. 440)
The middle cervical ganglion lies behind the vertebral artery
It lies in front of it; the inferior ganglion lies behind its commencement. (Last's p. 440)
The middle ganglion gives grey rami to C5 and C6
Superior to C1–4, inferior to C7–8. (Last's p. 440)
The cervical ganglia receive white rami from C8
No white rami enter them from cervical nerves. (Last's p. 440)
The cardiac branch of the left superior cervical ganglion goes to the superficial cardiac plexus
The other five go to the deep part. (Last's p. 441)
The inferior cervical ganglion sends visceral branches along the vertebral artery
Its vertebral plexus supplies only the vertebral branches, no viscera. (Last's p. 442)
The middle cervical ganglion supplies the upper oesophagus via the inferior thyroid artery
Also the lower larynx, trachea and hypopharynx. (Last's p. 442)
The external carotid plexus does not reach the otic ganglion
It supplies the submandibular and otic ganglia and pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 441-2)
Scalenus anterior is supplied by C4, 5, 6
By separate branches. (Last's p. 442)
Scalenus anterior is electrically silent in quiet respiration
It shows some EMG activity even then. (Last's p. 442)
The phrenic nerve passes in front of the vagus at the lung apex
Medial to the apex, onto the suprapleural membrane. (Last's p. 442)
The ascending cervical artery runs lateral to the phrenic nerve
It runs medial to it and is easily mistaken for it. (Last's p. 442)
The subclavian vein keeps its diameter in hypovolaemia
It adheres to surrounding connective tissue. (Last's p. 442)
The subclavian vein lies at a higher level than the scalenus anterior insertion
The slope of the rib puts it lower. (Last's p. 442)
Infraclavicular subclavian puncture starts 2 cm below the midpoint of the clavicle
Aiming at the jugular notch, through the clavipectoral fascia. (Last's p. 442)
The jugulo-omohyoid node lies below the inferior belly of omohyoid
It lies behind the vein above the inferior belly. (Last's p. 442)
The vertebral artery enters the foramen of C6 at the apex of the pyramidal space
It is the first subclavian branch. (Last's p. 444)
The middle cervical ganglion lies medial and posterior to the vertebral artery
It is medial and anterior; the stellate ganglion is medial, posterior and lower. (Last's p. 444)
There is no fascial roof across the pyramidal space
The subclavian artery passes behind the lateral expansion of prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 444)
The thoracic duct arches at a higher level than the inferior thyroid artery
It arches lower and further forward. (Last's p. 444)
The costocervical trunk arises from the second part
Behind scalenus anterior. (Last's p. 444)
The deep cervical artery runs behind semispinalis capitis
It runs in front of it to anastomose with the occipital. (Last's p. 444)
The dorsal scapular artery usually arises from the third part
It passes through the brachial plexus. (Last's p. 444)
The vertebral vein empties into the subclavian vein
It runs beneath the subclavian artery into the brachiocephalic vein. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus medius arises from the posterior tubercles of all cervical vertebrae
It inserts between the neck and subclavian groove of rib 1. (Last's p. 445)
Scalenus posterior inserts into the first rib
It inserts into the outer border of the second rib. (Last's p. 445)
The T1 anterior ramus occupies the subclavian groove of the first rib
The subclavian artery usually lies somewhat above. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus medius is supplied by C5–8 only
By C3–8. (Last's p. 445)
Senile facial wrinkles lie at right angles to the line of muscle pull
Incisions along them heal well. (Last's p. 445)
The facial muscles have a deep fascia
There is no deep fascia in the face. (Last's p. 445)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the pharynx below cricopharyngeus
(Last's p. 445)
Last's says the primary purpose of the facial muscles is expression
Their purpose is to control the orifices; expression is a side effect. (Last's p. 445)
Some lower palpebral fibres attach to the posterior lacrimal crest and lacrimal sac
The palpebral part inserts into the lateral palpebral raphe. (Last's p. 446)
The orbital part arises from the posterior lacrimal crest
It arises from the anterior lacrimal crest and frontal process of the maxilla. (Last's p. 446)
Gentle blinking does not reduce the volume of the conjunctival sac
Forcible closure does, spilling tears. (Last's p. 447)
In normal closure the medial upper lid descends before the lateral part
The lateral part comes down first, spreading tears medially. (Last's p. 447)
The incisive and mental slips are the deepest orbicularis oris fibres
The lip mucosa is firmly attached to them. (Last's p. 447)
At the modiolus the uppermost buccinator fibres decussate into the lower lip
The middle fibres decussate; uppermost and lowermost pass straight on. (Last's p. 447)
Tensor palati passes through the gap above the pterygomaxillary ligament
The band runs from the hamulus to the maxillary tuberosity. (Last's p. 447-8)
The parotid duct pierces buccinator opposite the second upper molar
Last's: opposite the third upper molar here. (Last's p. 448)
The lingual nerve rests on the mandible between the pterygomandibular raphe and mylohyoid attachments
It often grooves the bone. (Last's p. 448)
The buccal branch of the mandibular nerve is motor to buccinator
It is sensory (proprioceptive only for the muscle); motor is the facial nerve. (Last's p. 448)
Buccinator is relaxed when the cheeks are puffed out
Except in forcible blowing, as with a trumpet. (Last's p. 449)
Last's classifies buccinator as a muscle of mastication
It is an accessory muscle of mastication, not a proper one. (Last's p. 448)
The modiolus lies opposite the second upper premolar
Just lateral to the angle of the mouth. (Last's p. 449)
The infraorbital nerve lies deep to levator anguli oris
It lies between levator anguli oris and the overlying levator labii superioris. (Last's p. 449)
Depressor anguli oris arises from the oblique line of the mandible
Depressor labii inferioris arises deep to it. (Last's p. 449)
Mentalis depresses the lower lip
It elevates the chin skin and centre of the lower lip. (Last's p. 449)

questions.s: Concerning the facial nerve on the face (Last's):
o: The facial nerve divides into temporozygomatic and cervicofacial branches just before entering the parotid
(Last's p. 449)
The pes anserinus lies deep to the retromandibular vein
It lies superficial to the vein and external carotid. (Last's p. 449)
The marginal mandibular branch passes below the angle of the mandible in 20%
It crosses the facial artery and vein. (Last's p. 450)
Last's says the lower lip muscles are supplied by the cervical branch
That is called erroneous; the marginal mandibular supplies them. (Last's p. 450)

questions.s: Concerning the facial nerve and face sensation (Last's):
o: Upper zygomatic branches supply frontalis and the upper half of orbicularis oculi
Temporal branches are only important for wrinkling the forehead. (Last's p. 450)
The facial nerve carries proprioception from the facial muscles
It contains no sensory fibres on the face; proprioception travels in the trigeminal. (Last's p. 449)
The ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular nerves give five, three and three cutaneous branches
(Last's p. 450)
In herpes zoster the mandibular division is most often affected
It is less often affected than the other two. (Last's p. 450)
Pain from around the mouth synapses in the highest (pontine) part of the spinal nucleus
The onion-skin pattern does not match the divisional map exactly. (Last's p. 451)
The infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial lower lid
It supplies no lower lid skin, which is maxillary territory. (Last's p. 451)
The external nasal nerve emerges between the nasal bone and upper nasal cartilage
Its involvement in zoster warns of corneal involvement. (Last's p. 451)
The infraorbital labial branches supply the gum up to the first molar
Up to the second premolar. (Last's p. 451)
The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the hairless front of the temple
Level with the upper eyelid. (Last's p. 452)
The auriculotemporal nerve runs in front of the superficial temporal vessels
It ascends behind them. (Last's p. 452)
The buccal nerve gives cutaneous twigs before piercing buccinator
Supplying a thumbprint area of cheek. (Last's p. 452)
The supraorbital nerves supply the scalp only to the hairline
They supply up to the vertex. (Last's p. 451)
Each labial artery divides into two branches running in front of and behind the lip
They anastomose end to end in the midline. (Last's p. 452)
The transverse facial artery runs just below the parotid duct
It runs just above it. (Last's p. 452)
The external jugular has valves about 4 cm above the clavicle
It pierces the investing fascia a finger's breadth above mid-clavicle. (Last's p. 452)
The posterior branch of the retromandibular vein joins the facial vein
The anterior branch does; the posterior joins the posterior auricular to form the external jugular. (Last's p. 452)
Scalp skin is 3–7 mm thick, thickest in the occipital region
(Last's p. 452)
The two occipitalis muscles meet in the midline
The frontalis muscles meet; the occipitalis muscles do not. (Last's p. 453)
Only occipitalis has a bony attachment
Frontalis has no bony attachment. (Last's p. 453)
A subperiosteal haematoma of the scalp crosses suture lines
It outlines the bone because pericranium is firmly attached at sutures. (Last's p. 452)
Internal and external carotid branches anastomose most freely above the outer end of the eyebrow
(Last's p. 453)
Scalping causes necrosis of the vault bones
Most of their blood comes from the middle meningeal artery. (Last's p. 453)
The middle temporal vein grooves the squamous temporal bone vertically
The middle temporal artery pierces the temporalis fascia. (Last's p. 454)
There are lymph nodes within the scalp
There are none; drainage is to nodes outside. (Last's p. 454)
Temporalis is the only muscle that retracts the mandible
Its posterior fibres sweep over the zygomatic root. (Last's p. 455)
Temporalis inserts mainly into the outer surface of the coronoid process
Very little goes to the outer plate; the main insertion is the bevelled inner surface. (Last's p. 455)
Temporalis arises from the area between the inferior temporal line and the infratemporal crest
The fascia attaches to the superior line. (Last's p. 454)
The temporal and zygomatic bones meet at a suture sloping down and forwards
It slopes down and backwards. (Last's p. 454)
Last's describes masseter as three parts
Superficial, intermediate and deep, fused on the arch. (Last's p. 455)
The masseteric nerve runs between the superficial and intermediate parts
It runs between the deep and intermediate; the artery between superficial and intermediate. (Last's p. 455)
The masseter's main blood supply is a branch of the superficial temporal or transverse facial artery
Not the vessel with the masseteric nerve. (Last's p. 455)
The masseter's three parts are fused posteriorly at their insertion
They fuse anteriorly and diverge posteriorly. (Last's p. 455)
The stylomandibular ligament separates the parotid from the submandibular gland
And from medial pterygoid. (Last's p. 456)
Facial nerve branches emerge from the lateral surface of the parotid
They emerge from behind the anterior border. (Last's p. 456)
The styloid process separates the parotid from the internal jugular vein
And, deeper, the internal carotid. (Last's p. 456)
Last's endorses superficial and deep parotid lobes separated by the nerve
Last's says this is not a correct concept. (Last's p. 456)
From superficial to deep the parotid contains facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid
Nerves lie immediately superficial to the veins. (Last's p. 456)
The parotid duct opens opposite the first upper molar
It opens opposite the second upper molar, having pierced buccinator further back. (Last's p. 456)
The parotid fascia receives sensory fibres from the great auricular nerve
The gland itself from the auriculotemporal. (Last's p. 457)
The parotid gland has few ducts
It has many ducts, serous acini and fat cells. (Last's p. 457)
The stylomastoid artery lies slightly superficial to the facial nerve trunk
A guide to its proximity. (Last's p. 457)
The facial trunk is sought below stylohyoid and digastric
It is approached in front of the meatal cartilage, above stylohyoid and digastric. (Last's p. 457)
The parotid duct lies on a line from the intertragic notch to mid-philtrum
(Last's p. 456)
The accessory parotid lies below the parotid duct
It lies between the duct and the zygomatic arch. (Last's p. 456)
The roof lateral to the infratemporal crest is not bony
The temporal and infratemporal fossae communicate there. (Last's p. 457)
The posterior boundary of the infratemporal fossa is the styloid process
It is the upper carotid sheath. (Last's p. 457)
Some upper lateral pterygoid tendon fibres enter the articular disc
The rest inserts into the pterygoid fovea. (Last's p. 458)
The superficial head of medial pterygoid is the larger
The deep head is by far the larger. (Last's p. 458)
Medial pterygoid is supplied from the main mandibular trunk
Lateral pterygoid from the anterior division. (Last's p. 458-9)
The medial pterygoid plate lies between the two pterygoid muscles
The lateral plate does; the pharynx attaches to the medial plate. (Last's p. 458)
The two heads of medial pterygoid embrace the lower edge of lateral pterygoid
(Last's p. 459)
Medial pterygoid moves the mandible to its own side
It moves it towards the opposite side. (Last's p. 459)
The maxillary artery passes between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament
The auriculotemporal nerve lies above it. (Last's p. 459)
Branches of the second part of the maxillary artery pass through bony foramina
First and third part branches do; second part branches do not. (Last's p. 459)
The deep auricular artery passes between the meatal cartilage and bone
The anterior tympanic goes through the petrotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 459)
The pharyngeal branch of the maxillary artery is large
It is very small, in the palatovaginal canal. (Last's p. 459)
Last's calls the pterygoid plexus a peripheral heart
Pumped by lateral pterygoid when the mouth is actively opened. (Last's p. 460)
The pterygoid plexus is valveless
It is valved. (Last's p. 460)
The posterior superior alveolar gingival branch reaches forward to the first molar
Without piercing bone. (Last's p. 460)
The mylohyoid artery makes the mylohyoid groove
The accompanying small vein makes it. (Last's p. 460)

questions.s: Concerning the sphenomandibular ligament and mandibular nerve (Last's):
o: The sphenomandibular ligament is the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage
From the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula. (Last's p. 460)
The otic ganglion lies on the lateral surface of the mandibular nerve
It lies on its deep surface. (Last's p. 460)
The mandibular nerve lies 4 cm deep to the articular tubercle
Through the mandibular notch. (Last's p. 460)
The anterior division of the mandibular nerve is larger than the posterior
The anterior is small, mainly motor; the posterior large, mainly sensory. (Last's p. 460)
Styloid process and stylohyoid ligament lengths vary inversely
Both are second arch cartilage remnants. (Last's p. 466)
Stylopharyngeus arises lowest on the styloid process
It is deepest and arises highest; styloglossus arises from in front low down. (Last's p. 466)
The stylomandibular ligament runs from the vaginal process of the tympanic plate
To the angle of the mandible. (Last's p. 466)
The external carotid runs deep to stylopharyngeus
It runs superficial to stylopharyngeus and deep to digastric and stylohyoid. (Last's p. 466)
The pterygoid canal lies below and medial to the foramen rotundum
So the ganglion lies below and medial to V2. (Last's p. 466, 468)
The pharyngeal nerve reaches the nasopharynx through the pterygoid canal
It passes through the palatovaginal canal. (Last's p. 466, 469)
V2 deviates laterally in the inferior orbital fissure for about 1 cm
Before entering the infraorbital groove. (Last's p. 467)
The zygomatic nerve runs below V2 in the inferior orbital fissure
It runs above it. (Last's p. 467)
Last's says the connexion between V2 and the ganglion is a single large trunk
Not double, despite "ganglionic branches". (Last's p. 468)
The deep petrosal nerve arises from the carotid plexus in the carotid canal
It arises from the carotid nerve in the foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 468)
Every branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion carries sensory, secretomotor and sympathetic fibres
(Last's p. 469)
The pterygopalatine ganglion contains sympathetic cell bodies
Its only cell bodies are parasympathetic. (Last's p. 469)
The nasopalatine nerve was formerly the long sphenopalatine nerve
It supplies the septum and incisive gum. (Last's p. 469)
The greater palatine nerve supplies the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall
It supplies the posteroinferior quadrant; the lateral posterior superior nasal nerves the posterosuperior. (Last's p. 469)
Orbital branches supply orbitalis and the sphenoidal sinus
Via the inferior orbital fissure. (Last's p. 469)
In the pterygopalatine fossa the vessels lie posterior to the nerves
They generally lie anterior. (Last's p. 469)
The nasal mucocutaneous junction lies beyond the hair-bearing vestibule
(Last's p. 469)
The olfactory area extends below the superior concha
It lies over but not below it. (Last's p. 470)
The floor of the maxillary sinus often lies below the nasal floor
(Last's p. 470)
The nasal septum is usually exactly midline
It is nearly always deviated. (Last's p. 470)
Roof and septum may be only 2 mm apart at the roof
The cavity is pear-shaped in section. (Last's p. 470)
The superior concha is the longest
The inferior is the longest. (Last's p. 470)
The middle and superior conchae are joined anteriorly
They diverge posteriorly. (Last's p. 470)
The external nose is supplied at its base by the external nasal artery
The base by the dorsal nasal (ophthalmic); lower by the external nasal (anterior ethmoidal). (Last's p. 470)
The nasolacrimal duct opens about 2 cm behind the nostril
Into the inferior meatus. (Last's p. 471)
The sphenoidal ostium lies in the superior meatus
It is in the sphenoethmoidal recess, strictly in the roof. (Last's p. 471)
The auditory tube opening lies about 1 cm behind the inferior concha
In the nasopharynx, not the nasal cavity. (Last's p. 471)
The maxillary sinus opens at the anterior end of the semilunar hiatus
The frontal opens anteriorly; the maxillary near the posterior end. (Last's p. 472)
The sphenopalatine foramen lies behind the posterior end of the middle concha
Beneath the mucosa. (Last's p. 472)
Middle ethmoidal cell ostia lie low on the bulla
They usually open high on the bulla. (Last's p. 472)
Nasal lymphatics tend to run with the veins rather than arteries
(Last's p. 472)
Little's area is supplied by the septal branch of the inferior labial artery
The superior labial septal branch, sphenopalatine and greater palatine form Kiesselbach's plexus. (Last's p. 472)

questions.s: Concerning the nerves of the nasal walls (Last's):
o: Last's lists six nerves to the lateral nasal wall and four to the septum
(Last's p. 473)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve does not reach the nasal cavity
Some filaments supply the lower front of the lateral wall. (Last's p. 473)
The vestibule is supplied by the infraorbital nerve
Branches crept in from the face. (Last's p. 473)
The nasopalatine nerve runs in a groove on the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid
It runs in the groove on the vomer to the incisive canal. (Last's p. 473)
The inferior concha is a separate bone
The superior and middle are part of the ethmoid. (Last's p. 473)
The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid reaches further forward than the vomer
It falls short of the anterior end of the vomer. (Last's p. 473)
The uncinate process articulates with the base of the inferior concha
The semilunar hiatus lies between bulla and uncinate process. (Last's p. 473)
The nasolacrimal duct lies between the lacrimal bone and the ethmoid
It is enclosed between the lacrimal bone/frontal process of maxilla and the inferior concha. (Last's p. 473)
The ostium is the most sensitive part of a sinus
The main cavity is relatively insensitive. (Last's p. 474)
Gravity aids drainage of a normal sinus
Gravity plays no part; cilia move mucus spirally to the ostium. (Last's p. 474)
The maxillary ostium is 2–4 mm in diameter
A second smaller ostium often lies posteriorly. (Last's p. 474)
Maxillary sinus lymph drains to the deep cervical nodes directly
It drains to submandibular nodes. (Last's p. 474)
The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the premolars
When absent the anterior usually takes over. (Last's p. 474)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve leaves the infraorbital nerve on the orbital floor
It leaves in the infraorbital canal; the middle leaves on the floor. (Last's p. 474-5)
The greater palatine nerve supplies the back of the medial sinus wall
Through minute perforations. (Last's p. 475)
Tooth extraction fistulae into the sinus mostly require surgical closure
They mostly heal spontaneously. (Last's p. 474)
There may be from 3 to 18 ethmoidal air cells
Each with its own ostium. (Last's p. 475)
The ethmoidal labyrinth has its own bony roof
It is roofed by the orbital part of the frontal bone. (Last's p. 475)
The posterior ethmoidal foramen lies 1 cm behind the anterior
(Last's p. 475)
Posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the middle meatus
They drain into the superior meatus. (Last's p. 475)

questions.s: Concerning the sphenoidal and frontal sinuses (Last's):
o: The floor of a large sphenoidal sinus may be ridged by the pterygoid canal
And the palatovaginal canal. (Last's p. 476)
Sphenoidal sinus lymph drains to the submandibular nodes
It drains to retropharyngeal nodes. (Last's p. 476)
The frontal sinuses are the only sinuses absent at birth
They appear in the second year as migrated anterior ethmoidal cells. (Last's p. 476)
Frontal sinus lymph drains with the eyebrow skin to preauricular nodes
The sinus drains to submandibular nodes; the eyebrow to preauricular. (Last's p. 476)
In old age sinus enlargement is due to resorption of surrounding cancellous bone
Before adulthood it is due to bone enlargement. (Last's p. 476)
Frontal sinus venous drainage is into the inferior ophthalmic vein
Into diploic and superior ophthalmic veins. (Last's p. 476)
Early sinus enlargement coincides with eruption of the second dentition
(Last's p. 476)
The sphenoidal sinus is supplied by the anterior ethmoidal nerve
By the posterior ethmoidal and orbital branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion. (Last's p. 476)
The suctorial pad does not shrivel even with loss of other body fat
It lies between buccinator and the anterior border of masseter. (Last's p. 477)
The labial and buccal glands lie outside the facial muscles
Unlike the molar glands, they lie internal, in the mucosa. (Last's p. 477)
The alveolar–gingival mucosal junction lies 3–4 mm from the vestibular reflexion
Marked by an abrupt colour change. (Last's p. 477)
The buccal nerve usually supplies the upper gums
It spills over onto the lower jaw only. (Last's p. 477)
The periodontal ligament fibres run obliquely from bone towards the apex
Slinging the tooth against occlusal pressure. (Last's p. 478)
Lower molars have three roots
Upper molars have three; lower molars two. (Last's p. 478)
The anterior buccal root of the upper first molar is supplied by the middle superior alveolar nerve
(Last's p. 478)
Upper molars have five cusps
Upper four, lower five. (Last's p. 478)
Mandibular infiltration is usually effective only for the incisors
The rest need inferior alveolar block. (Last's p. 478)
In inferior alveolar block the needle is inserted behind the pterygomandibular raphe
In front of it, from the opposite premolars. (Last's p. 478)
In the posterior molar region the lingual mandibular plate is thinner than the buccal
Further forward the labial plate is thinner. (Last's p. 479)
An apical abscess of a lower second molar usually points in the mouth
Its apices lie below the mylohyoid line, so it points in the neck. (Last's p. 479)
Odontoblasts become active before ameloblasts
Though ameloblasts were there first. (Last's p. 479)
At eruption the root is fully formed
The crown is complete; the root only one-third formed. (Last's p. 479)
The canine is the last deciduous tooth to be replaced
Incisors first, then milk molars. (Last's p. 480)
An upper tooth erupts before its lower counterpart
A lower tooth precedes its upper opposite. (Last's p. 480)
The greater palatine artery runs lateral to the nerve
It enters the incisive foramen into the nose. (Last's p. 480)
The mucoperiosteum over the palatine horizontal plate is fixed by large Sharpey's fibres
Mucous glands separate mucosa and periosteum there; the bone is smooth. (Last's p. 480)
The greater palatine foramen lies level with the last molar
Between palatine bone and maxilla. (Last's p. 480)
The deciduous molars are replaced by permanent molars
They are replaced by premolars. (Last's p. 479)
The inferior constrictor is an elevator of the larynx

Its uppermost fibres pass very high on the pharyngeal raphe.
Last's calls this unexpected at first sight. (Last's p. 505)
Stylopharyngeus inserts essentially into the pharyngeal wall

Its essential insertion is into the larynx; Last's would rename it stylolaryngeus.
So too salpingo- and palatopharyngeus. (Last's p. 505)
Sternothyroid acts directly to depress the larynx
Sternohyoid and omohyoid act indirectly via the hyoid. (Last's p. 505)
Last's prefers tracheotomy to laryngotomy in an emergency

Emergency laryngotomy through the cricothyroid ligament is preferred.
There are no large midline vessels there. (Last's p. 504-5)
The medial wall is about 5 cm long

It runs from the anterior lacrimal crest back to the body of the sphenoid and optic canal.
The lateral wall is also about 5 cm. (Last's p. 505-6)
The lateral walls of the two orbits are parallel

The medial walls are parallel; the lateral walls make a right angle with each other.
Prolonged back they would meet at the pituitary fossa. (Last's p. 506)
The infraorbital margin is formed half and half by zygomatic bone and maxilla

They meet at a suture.
A suture leading to the infraorbital foramen closes in later life. (Last's p. 506)
The orbital floor is completed behind by the orbital process of the zygomatic bone

It is completed at the apex by the orbital process of the palatine bone.
The zygomatic completes it laterally in front. (Last's p. 506)
The orbital fascia is the periosteum of the orbit
At the back it is continuous with the dura and the optic nerve sheath. (Last's p. 505)
Orbital fat volume falls markedly with general weight loss

It remains very constant in volume despite changes in general body fat and fluid.
It cushions the eye. (Last's p. 505)
The marginal tubercle lies just inside the upper lateral orbital margin

It is on the zygomatic bone (of Whitnall).
The lateral palpebral ligament attaches to it. (Last's p. 506-7)
The inferior orbital fissure leads into the middle cranial fossa

It leads into the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae.
The superior orbital fissure leads into the middle fossa. (Last's p. 506)
The tarsal plates are dense fibrous tissue, not cartilage
They are thickenings of the orbital septum. (Last's p. 506-7)
The lateral palpebral ligament is stronger than the medial

The lateral is much thinner, fusing with the lateral palpebral raphe.
The medial anchors the tarsal plates to the anterior lacrimal crest. (Last's p. 507)
The angular vein lies superficial to orbicularis at the medial canthus
So does the termination of the facial artery. (Last's p. 507)
The lower lid is supplied by the infratrochlear nerve

The lower lid is supplied by the infraorbital nerve.
The infratrochlear supplies the upper lid with lacrimal, supraorbital and supratrochlear. (Last's p. 507)
Its goblet cells lie in islands mainly in the upper fornix
Elsewhere it has stratified squamous epithelium. (Last's p. 507)
The plica semilunaris lies at the lateral canthus

It lies near the medial canthus; its slack allows lateral deviation of the cornea.
It may be homologous with the third eyelid. (Last's p. 507)
The lacus lacrimalis lies between the plica and caruncle
Excess tears accumulate here before entering the canaliculi. (Last's p. 507)
The cornea is supplied by the nerves of the overlying lid skin

The cornea has a separate supply from long and short ciliary nerves.
The conjunctiva is supplied by the lid nerves. (Last's p. 507)
Ducts of the orbital part pass through the palpebral part
A dozen or more ducts open into the lateral superior fornix. (Last's p. 508)
Lid closure begins at the medial side of the upper lid
It begins laterally and moves medially, spreading tears. (Last's p. 508)
The posterior layer of the tear film is mucus from conjunctival goblet cells
The outer layer is oil; the middle aqueous. (Last's p. 508)
Blinking is produced by the orbital fibres of orbicularis oculi

It is produced by the palpebral fibres and does not diminish the conjunctival sac.
Orbital fibres compress the sac. (Last's p. 508)

questions.s: Concerning the lacrimal sac and duct (Last's):
o: The lacrimal sac is really the blind upper end of the nasolacrimal duct
Its wall has much elastic tissue. (Last's p. 508)
The nasolacrimal duct slopes downwards and medially
It slopes downwards and laterally, conforming with the nasal cavity. (Last's p. 508)
The nasolacrimal duct opens rather more than 2 cm behind the nostril
It opens in the inferior meatus; it is 2 cm long with a 3.5 mm lumen. (Last's p. 508)
When orbicularis relaxes the sac is drawn open
Contraction draws the sac open and sucks tears in; relaxation lets it recoil and pump them down. (Last's p. 508)
Orbitalis lies on the orbital floor
It is smooth muscle of little human interest. (Last's p. 508)
The eyes lie symmetrically in the axis of the orbit
They do not; the eyes face forward in parallel while the orbits diverge. (Last's p. 508)
The optic nerve and ocular muscles arise at the back of the medial wall
They pass laterally, not straight forwards, to the eye. (Last's p. 508)
Levator palpebrae superioris is counted among the six extraocular muscles
The six are four recti and two obliques; levator and orbitalis are extra. (Last's p. 508)

questions.s: The superior orbital fissure and tendinous ring (Last's):
o: The superior orbital fissure is retort-shaped with the broad end medially
The tendinous ring surrounds the bulb of the retort and the optic foramen. (Last's p. 509)
Levator palpebrae superioris arises from the tendinous ring
Levator and superior oblique arise from bone above the ring; the four recti from the ring. (Last's p. 509)
The only nasociliary branches leaving the cone pass beneath superior oblique
They are the posterior and anterior ethmoidal and infratrochlear nerves. (Last's p. 509)
The trochlear nerve passes through the tendinous ring
Lacrimal, frontal and trochlear pass outside the ring and stay outside the cone. (Last's p. 509)
Its nerve may pierce the superior rectus to reach it
The superior division branch pierces superior rectus or passes on its medial side. (Last's p. 509)
Its smooth muscle part's sympathetic cell bodies lie in the inferior cervical ganglion
They lie in the superior cervical ganglion. (Last's p. 509)
Facial nerve paralysis does not cause ptosis

It prevents screwing up the lids.
Complete III palsy gives complete ptosis. (Last's p. 509)
Its weaker posterior tendon flange attaches to the skin of the upper lid
The front flange reaches the skin; the weaker posterior flange attaches to the superior fornix. (Last's p. 509)
The superior and medial recti also arise from the dural sheath of the optic nerve
This is why retrobulbar neuritis can cause pain on eye movement. (Last's p. 509)
The lateral rectus has the shortest origin of the recti
Its origin is C-shaped and longer than the others, bridging the fissure. (Last's p. 509)
The medial rectus passes below the superior oblique
It runs along the medial wall to insert in front of the equator. (Last's p. 509)
An expansion from the sheath of the inferior rectus passes below the inferior oblique
It passes above the inferior oblique into the lower lid. (Last's p. 509)
The trochlea lies a few millimetres behind the superomedial orbital margin
It is attached beneath the frontal sinus. (Last's p. 510)
The superior oblique tendon passes above the superior rectus to its insertion
It passes under the superior rectus to the posterosuperior quadrant. (Last's p. 510)
The inferior oblique usually leaves no mark on the bone
Occasionally a pit is seen near the nasolacrimal canal. (Last's p. 510)
The inferior oblique passes above the inferior rectus
It passes below the inferior rectus, then between lateral rectus and sclera. (Last's p. 510)

questions.s: Concerning the fascial sheath of the eye (Last's):
o: The medial check ligament attaches to the posterior lacrimal crest
The lateral check ligament attaches to the marginal tubercle at the same level. (Last's p. 511)
The eye rests on the floor of the orbit
It is suspended by the suspensory ligament, nearer the superior margin. (Last's p. 511)
The maxilla can be removed up to the marginal tubercle without the eye descending
Above this the suspensory attachments are lost and diplopia results. (Last's p. 511)
Contracting recti displace the eye backwards
Neither resting nor contracting recti do; it rotates about a fixed centre. (Last's p. 511)
Seven nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure
III (two divisions), IV, VI, and lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary. (Last's p. 511)
The frontal nerve gives branches to the extraocular muscles
Frontal and infraorbital nerves give only periosteal twigs; they use the orbit for transit. (Last's p. 511)
The zygomatic nerve gives its lacrimal communication before entering its foramen
It runs along the lower lateral wall to the zygomatico-orbital foramen. (Last's p. 512)
The ophthalmic artery crosses the optic nerve from medial to lateral
It crosses obliquely superficially from lateral to medial, with nasociliary and superior ophthalmic vein just behind. (Last's p. 512)

questions.s: Nerves inside and outside the cone (Last's):
o: The lacrimal nerve is the smallest of the three main V1 branches
It runs along the upper border of lateral rectus. (Last's p. 512)
The trochlear nerve lies lateral to the frontal nerve
It lies medial to the frontal nerve, crossing the origin of levator. (Last's p. 512)
The inferior division of III is the larger
It gives nerves to inferior rectus, medial rectus and inferior oblique. (Last's p. 512)
The nerve to medial rectus passes above the optic nerve
It passes below the optic nerve. (Last's p. 512)

questions.s: Concerning the nasociliary nerve in the orbit (Last's):
o: It runs lateral to the ophthalmic artery after entering the ring
It then crosses above the optic nerve, behind the artery, from lateral to medial. (Last's p. 513)
It reaches the medial wall between the medial rectus and inferior rectus
It approaches the medial wall between the superior oblique and superior rectus. (Last's p. 513)
The infratrochlear nerve supplies the lacrimal sac
It passes above the medial palpebral ligament to the upper lid and bridge of the nose. (Last's p. 513)
The posterior ethmoidal nerve is the most proximal branch of the nasociliary in the cone
It is the most distal of the branches within the cone. (Last's p. 513)
It lies about 8 mm from the apex of the orbit
That is a third of the way to the eye, lateral to the optic nerve, 2 mm across. (Last's p. 513)
Dividing its sensory root abolishes the conjunctival reflex
It abolishes the corneal reflex but not the conjunctival reflex. (Last's p. 513)
Its sympathetic root passes through the ring just below the nasociliary nerve
It carries vasoconstrictor fibres to the eye's vessels. (Last's p. 513)
Most of its postganglionic fibres supply sphincter pupillae
Only 3% supply the sphincter (about 50 motor units); the vast majority supply the ciliary muscle. (Last's p. 513)
The long ciliary nerves pierce the sclera medial to the short ciliary nerves
There are two of them. (Last's p. 513)
The long ciliary nerves help alter the shape of the lens

Only the short ciliary nerves constrict the pupil and alter the lens.
Both carry corneal sensation. (Last's p. 514)
Last's orbit chapter says there are a dozen or more short ciliary nerves

The cranial nerve chapter says 8–10.
Each contains fibres from all three roots. (Last's p. 513, 632)
The short ciliary nerves run in the subretinal space
They run in the suprachoroidal space. (Last's p. 513)
The optic nerve joins it from above in the optic canal
Both lie in a tubular prolongation of dura. (Last's p. 514)
The supraorbital artery is one of its terminal branches
Its terminal branches are the supratrochlear and dorsal nasal; the supraorbital arises far back. (Last's p. 514)
The central artery is its first and smallest branch
It is also by far the most important; it is an end artery. (Last's p. 514)
The central artery anastomoses freely with the posterior ciliary arteries
There is no anastomosis between the two sets. (Last's p. 514)
The superior ophthalmic vein communicates with the angular vein
It drains directly into the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 514)
The inferior ophthalmic vein drains only into the cavernous sinus
It drains through the inferior orbital fissure into the pterygoid plexus. (Last's p. 514)
Orbital lymph drains to preauricular and parotid nodes
Then to the upper deep cervical nodes. (Last's p. 514)
The ocular muscles have unusually few muscle spindles
They have an unusually high proportion of spindles and nerve fibres. (Last's p. 514)
Superior and inferior recti both turn the eye in
Three recti (medial, superior, inferior) turn the eye in. (Last's p. 514)
The obliques' vertical actions are greatest with the eye turned out

They become effective when the eye is turned in.
The recti act best with the eye turned out. (Last's p. 515)
The inferior oblique produces extorsion
12 o'clock moves to 11 on the right cornea with inferior rectus and oblique. (Last's p. 515)
The para-abducent nucleus projects to the opposite abducent nucleus
It projects to the abducent nucleus of the same side and the opposite oculomotor nucleus via the MLF. (Last's p. 515)
Nystagmus is named from the direction of the quick phase
Usually the slow drift is away from, the quick jerk towards, gaze. (Last's p. 515)
Iced water in an unconscious patient deviates the eyes away from the irrigated side
It induces conjugate deviation to the same side. (Last's p. 515)
In III palsy the consensual reflex in the opposite eye is preserved
The affected pupil is dilated and unreactive. (Last's p. 516)
In IV palsy the head tilts towards the affected side
It tilts towards the opposite shoulder to counter extorsion. (Last's p. 516)

questions.s: Concerning the coats of the eye (Last's):
o: The sclera can be regarded as an expansion of the dural sheath
The choroid corresponds to arachnoid and pia; the retina to brain. (Last's p. 516)
The sclera is thickest at the entrance of the optic nerve
It is thinnest there, forming the sieve-like lamina cribrosa. (Last's p. 516)
Chronic glaucoma causes the lamina cribrosa to bulge backwards
This is cupping of the disc. (Last's p. 516)
The sclera forms the posterior two-thirds of the eyeball
It forms the posterior five-sixths. (Last's p. 516)
The venae vorticosae pierce the sclera just behind the coronal equator
There are four or five of them, draining the choroid. (Last's p. 516-17)
The episclera is avascular
The sclera is almost avascular; the episclera is vascular and causes circumcorneal injection. (Last's p. 517)
The radial ciliary muscle fibres attach to the scleral spur
The spur bounds the canal of Schlemm. (Last's p. 517)
The corneal epithelium is about twenty cell layers thick

It is a very regular stratified squamous epithelium of about five layers.
The stroma has over 200 lamellae. (Last's p. 517)
Descemet's membrane is produced by the corneal endothelium
It is the posterior limiting layer. (Last's p. 517)
The cornea is supplied mainly by the long ciliary nerves
Last's: mainly by the short ciliary nerves, with a few fibres in the long ciliaries. (Last's p. 517)
Last's routes the corneal reflex through the main sensory nucleus of V
Trigeminal ganglion (no synapse), main sensory nucleus, reticular neurons, both facial nuclei. (Last's p. 517)
The cornea takes no oxygen directly from the air
It takes oxygen directly from the air, plus diffusion from aqueous and limbal vessels. (Last's p. 517)

questions.s: Concerning the ciliary body and iris (Last's):
o: There are about seventy ciliary processes
They radiate about 2 mm from the anterior margin; the processes are white, the grooves black. (Last's p. 518)
The ciliary muscle's opponent is the dilator pupillae
It has no opponent; elastic recoil of the suprachoroid lamina re-tenses the ligament. (Last's p. 518)
Sphincter and dilator pupillae are derived from neural ectoderm
The ciliary muscle is mesodermal. (Last's p. 518)
A blue iris contains abundant pigment cells
Absent pigment cells give blue by light diffusion in front of the black posterior surface. (Last's p. 518)
Pupillary fibres lie on the dorsal surface of the oculomotor trunk
They are supplied by sheath vessels, so spared in diabetic infarction but affected by aneurysm. (Last's p. 518-19)
The accommodation pathway relays through the pretectal nucleus
It reaches the Edinger–Westphal nucleus from the frontal eye field without the pretectal nucleus. (Last's p. 519)
Last's expresses doubt about the pretectal explanation of the Argyll Robertson pupil
It fails to explain why the pupil is small. (Last's p. 519)
Horner's syndrome above the superior cervical ganglion abolishes facial sweating
If the lesion is above the ganglion there is no loss of sweating. (Last's p. 519)
The macula lies about 3 mm lateral to the optic disc
It is of comparable size to the disc and free of vessels. (Last's p. 520)
In retinal detachment the pigment layer separates from the choroid
The pigment cells stay attached; the rods, cones and inner layers detach. (Last's p. 520)
Layer 8 contains the ganglion cell nuclei
Layer 4 holds rod and cone nuclei; layer 6 bipolar nuclei. (Last's p. 520)
The rods and cones are supplied by branches of the central artery
They are supplied by diffusion from choroidal capillaries; the central artery supplies bipolar and ganglion cells. (Last's p. 521)
The central retinal vein joins the superior ophthalmic vein
It leaves via the optic disc. (Last's p. 521)
The ora serrata lies at the equator
It lies halfway between the equator and the corneoscleral junction. (Last's p. 519)
Most refraction occurs at the air–cornea junction
Light then passes through aqueous, lens and vitreous. (Last's p. 521)
The upper and lower temporal retinal arteries cross the macula
They curve up and down to clear the macula. (Last's p. 521)

questions.s: Concerning the chambers, lens and vitreous (Last's):
o: The posterior surface of the lens is more convex than the anterior
The lens is about 10 mm in diameter. (Last's p. 522)
The lens capsule is thickest at the posterior pole

It is thickest anteriorly near the circumference.
The capsular epithelium lies anteriorly. (Last's p. 522)
The vitreous body occupies the posterior four-fifths of the eyeball

It is attached to the optic disc and just in front of the ora serrata.
The hyaloid canal marks the embryonic hyaloid artery. (Last's p. 522)
The anterior chamber is about 1 mm deep
It is about 3 mm deep. (Last's p. 522)

questions.s: Lymph drainage of the head and neck (Last's):
o: A single lingual node may lie on the outer surface of hyoglossus
A single buccal node may lie on buccinator. (Last's p. 522)
Upper deep cervical nodes drain the thyroid gland
The lower group drains the face, anterior scalp, anterior tongue, lower pharynx, larynx, thyroid and mediastinum. (Last's p. 523)
Upper deep cervical nodes drain the tonsil and the back of the tongue
They also drain the ear, nose, sinuses and upper pharynx and larynx. (Last's p. 523)
The right jugular trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct
The left trunk usually joins the thoracic duct; the right reaches the right lymphatic duct or brachiocephalic vein. (Last's p. 523)
It contains no hyaline cartilage
Both bones and the disc have the same fibrocartilage; it is atypical. (Last's p. 523)
The disc is thickest at its centre
It is thinnest at the centre and thickest around the edges. (Last's p. 523)
The posterior part of the disc has crinkled fibres
They elongate and recoil, as the posterior attachment is nearer the temporal bone. (Last's p. 523)
The capsule is attached posteriorly to the articular tubercle
It is attached anteriorly just in front of the articular tubercle, and posteriorly to the squamotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 523)
The sphenomandibular ligament stays constant in length in all jaw positions
Its lower attachment is at the axis of rotation. (Last's p. 523)
The lateral ligament is tightest in the rest position
It is most relaxed at rest and tightened by movement away from rest. (Last's p. 523)
Upward dislocation through the fossa roof is possible but very rare
A blow on the drooping chin usually closes or opens the mouth further. (Last's p. 524)
Forward TMJ dislocation is held by spasm of the anterior fibres of temporalis
It is held by spasm of the posterior deep fibres of masseter. (Last's p. 524)
At rest the teeth are separated by 3–4 mm
This is the rest position. (Last's p. 524)
Retraction is produced by the anterior fibres of temporalis
It is produced by the lowest horizontal fibres that hook over the root of the zygomatic process. (Last's p. 524)
The axis of jaw opening passes through the mandibular foramina
The sphenomandibular ligaments act like the ropes of a swing. (Last's p. 524-5)
In the unconscious patient the jaw drops by gliding in the upper compartment
It drops by hinge movement only in the lower compartment, and the tongue swings back. (Last's p. 525)

questions.s: Concerning the floor of the mouth and swallowing (Last's):
o: Geniohyoid and stylohyoid set the anteroposterior position of the hyoid
The mylohyoid raphe lengthens or shortens like a concertina. (Last's p. 525)
The hyoid rises before the larynx in swallowing
The larynx and pharynx first move up to the hyoid, then all rise together. (Last's p. 525)
The epiglottis returns by its own elastic recoil
Its framework is elastic cartilage. (Last's p. 525)
A small liquid bolus passes in a single midline channel over the epiglottis
It is split by the inverted epiglottis into two lateral food channels. (Last's p. 525)
The anteroinferior wall of the external meatus is the longest
Because the membrane lies obliquely; the posterosuperior wall is shortest. (Last's p. 526)
The outer two-thirds of the meatus is cartilaginous
The outer third is cartilage, the inner two-thirds bone. (Last's p. 526)
Ceruminous glands lie in the cartilaginous part of the meatus
So do hairs and sebaceous glands. (Last's p. 526)
The deep auricular artery enters the meatus through the petrotympanic fissure
It enters through the squamotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 526)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the external ear (Last's):
o: The great auricular nerve supplies the whole cranial surface of the auricle
With a little overlap from the lesser occipital at the top, plus the lower lateral surface. (Last's p. 526)
The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the lower part of the lateral surface of the auricle
It supplies the upper lateral surface and most of the meatal skin. (Last's p. 526)
Facial nerve twigs reach posterior meatal skin via the tympanic plexus
Vagal twigs also spill over, extending onto the mastoid. (Last's p. 526)
The auricular cartilage extends into the lobule
It does not; the lobule is skin with fibrofatty tissue. (Last's p. 526)
It forms by interposition of part of the second pouch into the first
Hence its mixed nerve supply. (Last's p. 526)
The tympanic cavity is about 5 mm in diameter
It is about 15 mm in diameter, shaped like a tilted biconcave lens. (Last's p. 526-7)
The tympanic membrane lies at 55° to the external meatus
It faces downwards and forwards as well as laterally. (Last's p. 527)
The outer fibres of the drum are circumferential
The superficial (lateral) fibres are radial; the deep (medial) circumferential. (Last's p. 527)

questions.s: Concerning the walls of the middle ear (Last's):
o: The trochleariform process lies just below the anterior end of the facial canal
It is the posterior end of the tensor tympani canal. (Last's p. 528)
The round window lies above and behind the promontory
The oval window is above and behind; the round window below and behind. (Last's p. 528)
The internal opening of the tympanic canaliculus is at the anterior end of the floor
The tympanic branch of IX enters here. (Last's p. 528)
The canal for tensor tympani lies below the bony auditory tube
It is the upper, smaller canal; the tube is the lower, larger one. (Last's p. 528)
The ossicles begin to ossify in the twelfth week
They are already almost adult size then. (Last's p. 528)
The chorda tympani crosses lateral to the neck of the malleus

It crosses medial to the neck.
The neck lies against the pars flaccida. (Last's p. 528)
The anterior ligament of the malleus continues as the sphenomandibular ligament
It passes through the squamotympanic fissure to the spine of the sphenoid. (Last's p. 529)
The anterior limb of the stapes is longer and more curved than the posterior
The anterior limb is shorter and less curved. (Last's p. 529)
Tensor tympani's motor fibres pass near the otic ganglion without relay
Their cell bodies are in the trigeminal motor nucleus. (Last's p. 529)
Tensor tympani inserts into the lower end of the handle of the malleus
It inserts into the upper end of the handle, after bending round the trochleariform process. (Last's p. 529)
Stapedius inserts into the back of the neck of the stapes
It tilts the footpiece so its anterior margin cants towards the tympanic cavity. (Last's p. 529)
The middle ear muscles damp high-pitched sound
Last's: they damp overvibration from low-pitched sound. (Last's p. 529)

questions.s: Vessels and nerves of the middle ear (Last's):
o: Middle ear veins drain to the superior petrosal sinus
Others go through the squamotympanic fissure to the pterygoid plexus. (Last's p. 529)
The largest middle ear arteries come from the internal carotid
Most come from external carotid branches: anterior tympanic and stylomastoid. (Last's p. 529)
Middle ear lymph drains to retropharyngeal nodes
Also to parotid and upper deep cervical nodes. (Last's p. 529)
Jacobson's nerve is a branch of the facial nerve
It is the tympanic branch of IX. (Last's p. 529)

questions.s: Concerning the tympanic plexus and facial nerve in the ear (Last's):
o: The lesser petrosal nerve emerges from a hiatus lateral to the greater petrosal nerve
It leaves the middle ear by a canaliculus in the anterior wall above the auditory tube. (Last's p. 530)
The facial nerve runs within the middle ear cavity
It is not in the cavity but runs through the petrous bone laterally, posteriorly then downwards. (Last's p. 530)
In the internal meatus course the facial nerve lies above the vestibule
With the cochlea in front and the semicircular canals behind. (Last's p. 530)
The chorda tympani pierces the posterior wall medial to the pyramid
It pierces the posterior wall lateral to the pyramid. (Last's p. 530)
It is over 3 cm long
The bony part is over 1 cm, the cartilaginous over 2 cm; the reverse of the external meatus. (Last's p. 530)
The isthmus lies at the pharyngeal end of the tube
It is at the bony orifice, posteromedial to the spine of the sphenoid. (Last's p. 530)
In section the cartilage resembles an inverted J with the long limb posterior
The posterior flange forms the tubal elevation. (Last's p. 530-1)
The bony part of the tube contains many mucous glands
Like the other bony cavities it contains no glands; it is kept moist by evaporation. (Last's p. 530)
Last's gives its downward slope as 30° in the ear section

In the skull section (p. 650) Last's gives about 20°.
It runs forward and medially at 45°. (Last's p. 530, 650)
Its cilia beat towards the middle ear
They beat towards the nasopharynx, protecting the middle ear. (Last's p. 531)
The nervus spinosus supplies its cartilaginous part
The pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion supplies the ostium; the tympanic plexus the bony part. (Last's p. 531)
Its arterial supply is from the facial and lingual arteries
It is supplied by the ascending pharyngeal and middle meningeal arteries. (Last's p. 531)

questions.s: Concerning the mastoid antrum and air cells (Last's):
o: The antrum may be up to 1 cm in diameter
When large it is covered by thin bone, when small by thick. (Last's p. 531)
Mastoid air cells first appear after puberty
They burrow out during the first year. (Last's p. 531)
A "false bottom" may separate squamous and petrous air cells
The squamous part overlies the petrous part. (Last's p. 531)
The mastoid antrum is roofed by the floor of the posterior fossa
It is roofed by the tegmen tympani. (Last's p. 531)
The apex of the modiolus points towards the canal for tensor tympani
Its base lies at the fundus of the internal meatus. (Last's p. 532)
The spiral lamina is widest in the apical turn
It is widest in the basal turn and narrowest apically. (Last's p. 532)
The scalae vestibuli and tympani communicate at the helicotrema
This is at the cupola around the blind apex of the cochlear duct. (Last's p. 532)
The aqueduct of the cochlea is closed in life
It is patent; perilymph drains through it into the subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 532-3)
The saccule lies in the spherical recess
It is the anteroinferior concavity; the utricle lies in the elliptical recess. (Last's p. 533)
Perilymph escapes through the aqueduct of the vestibule

No fluid passes; it is plugged by the endolymphatic duct and a vein.
Last's calls it badly named. (Last's p. 534)
The cochlear recess transmits nerves to the basal end of the cochlear duct
It lies just behind the basal end of the spiral lamina. (Last's p. 534)
The vestibule is about 10 mm long
It is about 3 mm wide, 6 mm long and 5 mm high. (Last's p. 533)
The ampulla of the anterior canal lies laterally
Its convexity forms the arcuate eminence; it lies highest. (Last's p. 534)
The ampulla of the lateral canal lies posteriorly
It lies anteriorly and bulges the medial wall of the aditus above the facial canal. (Last's p. 534)
The posterior canal of one side is parallel with the anterior canal of the other
Both lie at 45° to the sagittal plane. (Last's p. 534)
The common crus is about 10 mm long
It is about 4 mm long; there are five openings into the vestibule. (Last's p. 534)
The basilar membrane is widest at the apex
0.4 mm at the apex, 0.2 mm at the base; over 3 cm long. (Last's p. 534)
The vestibular membrane lies on the basal side of the basilar membrane
Reissner's membrane lies on the apical side, making the duct triangular. (Last's p. 534)
The inner ear is practically full adult size at birth
It is buried in the petrous bone. (Last's p. 531)
The stria vascularis is formed by the inner epithelial layer
It is formed where the outer vascular fibrous layer adheres to the endosteum. (Last's p. 534)

questions.s: Concerning the spiral organ and vestibular receptors (Last's):
o: The hearing "hairs" are modified microvilli (stereocilia)
They are overlaid by the tectorial membrane. (Last's p. 534)
Last's describes about 15 000 outer and 3500 inner hair cells
Last's gives a single outer row of about 3500 cells and inner three to five rows of up to 15 000. (Last's p. 534)
The endolymphatic sac is the site of absorption of endolymph
It projects beneath the dura of the posterior fossa. (Last's p. 534)
The macula of the utricle lies on its medial wall
The saccule's macula is on its medial wall; the utricle's on its floor. (Last's p. 534)

questions.s: Concerning the semicircular ducts and labyrinthine vessels (Last's):
o: The semicircular ducts are only a quarter the calibre of the bony canals
Except at the ampullae, which they almost fill. (Last's p. 534)
The labyrinthine vein drains into the superior petrosal sinus
It leaves the internal meatus to join the inferior petrosal sinus. (Last's p. 535)
The vein in the aqueduct of the vestibule joins the superior petrosal sinus
The vein in the aqueduct of the cochlea joins the inferior petrosal sinus. (Last's p. 535)
The upper vestibular division supplies the ampulla of the posterior duct
The lower division supplies it through the foramen singulare. (Last's p. 535)
